title: When the misls quarreled
hookLine: as danger faded, rivalry grew between the misls

cards: A family pulls together beautifully at a funeral or in a hospital waiting room. Everyone brings food, nobody keeps score. Then the crisis passes, and months later two siblings aren't speaking over who got the good china.
Sikh histories tell a story with the same shape. For a long time the misls were hunted, and they rode together because they had to.
Then the hunters grew weaker, the misls held land, and the old enemy was no longer at the gate.

teach.b: While the danger was great, Sikh histories say, the bands needed one another. They met as the Sarbat Khalsa, agreed a gurmata, and rode under shared leaders.

But once the misls held territory, each chief had something to lose, and something to gain at a neighbor's expense: border villages, river crossings, revenue, marriages that tied one house to another, or failed to.
The quarrels were not about faith. The chiefs bowed at the same Harmandir and heard the same scripture.

teach.h: LAND, PRIDE AND WHO WOULD LEAD.
teach.b: They were about land, pride and who would lead. One story shows it.

Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the builder of yesterday's towers, was, Sikh histories say, pushed out of his lands for a time by rival chiefs who had once ridden beside him, and he lived beyond the Sutlej until he could come back.
Other misls fought, made peace and fought again, and the gatherings at Amritsar grew harder to hold together. Set that beside their scripture.
In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1299, the singer says, in paraphrase, that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he has come to get along with everyone.
Hearing it didn't stop the quarrels. That's the honest part of this story: unity under pressure is real, but it's easier than unity at ease.

how: Sikh histories tell the misl rivalries frankly, and Sikhs read Guru Arjan's hymn on Ang 1299 of the Guru Granth Sahib about having no enemy and no stranger.

games.q: you're a misl chief. the old enemy is weaker now and your band holds good land. your neighbor's band holds the river crossing you need. what happens next, in the story Sikh histories tell?
o: you share the crossing and meet at Amritsar as before.
the bands start fighting each other over land and pride.
you hand your land to the neighbor.
games.why: as danger faded, rivalry grew. the chiefs who had ridden together fought over territory, though they shared the same scripture.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've drifted into competing with or quietly resenting, a sibling, a coworker, an old friend, and remember a time you were on the same side.
Ask what the rivalry is really about, maybe something small, land, pride, who leads, and think of one move that would cool it; Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Sarbat Khalsa, the gathering that once bound the misls. Once danger faded, they quarreled over land and leadership, even sharing one scripture. This week: the Karorsinghia, the Shaheedan, the Phulkian states, twice a year at Amritsar, the bungas, the Ramgarhia towers, and the quarrels. Today's word.
